Continue the Poutine League employee-facing Power Apps code app build — this is Phase 1 of the agreed phased plan, stacked on top of the just-completed Phase 0 layer (PR #26, branch rpothin-literate-disco: scaffold, all 11 Dataverse data sources wired, nav shell, design tokens).

Read first: code-apps/employee-app/memory-bank.md (Phase 0 state + known blocker), the session plan in this repo's plan.md if present, code-apps/employee-app/PRODUCT.md, root PRODUCT.md, root ARCHITECTURE.md (data model section 1 especially — Restaurant, PoutineSubmission, Tag tables and the Employee security role privilege matrix), and code-apps/DESIGN.md (design tokens already ported to code-apps/employee-app/src/styles/tokens.css — reuse them, don't redefine).

Build Phase 1 — 'Submit a poutine':
- Create-submission form: restaurant/place name + address (lookup existing Restaurant record or create a new one), poutine name/description, price, photo, tags (multi-select against the seeded Tag table).
- Enforce the hard cap of 5 active submissions per employee (client-side check against PoutineSubmission count for the current SystemUser — the generated MicrosoftDataverseService/Model in src/generated/ already covers all needed tables including rpo_poutinesubmission, rpo_restaurant, rpo_tag, and systemuser).
- A 'My submissions' list/management view (edit/withdraw own drafts).
- No AI moderation integration — submissions are created directly (the moderation/review agent flow is explicitly out of scope for this app).
- Use the existing NavShell/EmptyState components and design tokens; wire the Submit screen for real instead of the current placeholder.
- Use the generated Dataverse service methods for all data access — never hand-edit src/generated/ or use fetch/axios directly.

Gate: run `make app-gate` (lint + test) from the repo root before considering this done, and `npm run build` inside code-apps/employee-app. Known environment blocker: `pac code push` will still fail with CodeAppOperationNotAllowedInEnvironment (HTTP 403) until an environment admin enables 'Power Apps code apps' in the Power Platform Admin Center for the raphaelpothin-sandbox environment — this is expected and does not block this phase's local build/lint/dev work. Do not attempt to work around it.

When done: commit to this branch, run the mandatory Entire traceability protocol (make entire-observe -> entire-link-dry -> entire-link-apply/entire-link-apply-unsafe -> entire-stack-finalize) before finalizing, push, and open a PR based on rpothin-literate-disco (this branch) — not main — since this is a stacked layer per the repo's gh-stack convention.
I'll start by reading the key context documents to understand Phase 0 state and requirements.

1. # Poutine League — Architecture
2. 
3. This document describes the initial **Power Platform-centric technical architecture** for Poutine League, derived from the functional vision in [`PRODUCT.md`](./PRODUCT.md). It captures decisions made so far and flags open questions to resolve during implementation.
4. 
5. The architecture leans **exclusively** on four Power Platform building blocks:
6. 
7. | Building block | Role in this product |
8. |---|---|
9. | **Dataverse** | System of record for the data model, plus the mechanism for injecting sample/demo data. |
10. | **Power Automate cloud flows** | Non-AI, deterministic backend processes (scheduling, aggregation, notifications, geocoding). |
11. | **Power Apps code apps** | Front-end experiences (employee app + admin app). |
12. | **Copilot Studio agents (GitHub Copilot harness)** | AI agentic experiences — one interactive conversational agent, and specialized headless agents for backend AI reasoning. |
13. 
14. > [!NOTE]
15. > This document favors a **single Dev environment with one unmanaged solution** for the demo. Multi-environment promotion is intentionally out of scope for the live demo (see [ALM & environments](#alm--environments)), even though a deterministic CD pipeline already exists in this repo as a forward-looking illustration.
16. 
17. ## 1. Data model (Dataverse)
18. 
19. Dataverse is the single system of record. All entities below are custom tables unless noted otherwise.
20. 
21. | Table | Purpose | Key fields (indicative) |
22. |---|---|---|
23. | **Restaurant** | A Montreal restaurant/place where a poutine was found. | Name, address, geocoded latitude/longitude, city area/neighborhood. |
24. | **Poutine Submission** | A submitted poutine, owned by the submitting employee. | Name/description, price, photo (Dataverse file/image column), tags, status (`Draft` → `Submitted` → `In Review` → `Approved`/`Rejected`), lookup to Restaurant, lookup to submitter (system user). |
25. | **Tag** | Descriptive tag (classic, smoked meat, vegan, spicy, …). | Name. Many-to-many with Poutine Submission. |
26. | **Try** | An employee self-declaring they tried a poutine. | Lookup to Poutine Submission, lookup to employee (system user), timestamp. |
27. | **Review** | Rating + comment left after a Try. | Star rating (1–5), comment text, lookup to Try/Poutine Submission, lookup to reviewer (system user), AI-assessed helpfulness score (nullable, populated by the review-scoring backend agent). |
28. | **Season** | A seasonal contest period (winter/spring/summer/autumn). | Start/end date, status (`Active`/`Closed`). |
29. | **Category** | A leaderboard category (Best Seller, Top Poutine, Best Supporter, Best Critic, + future ones). | Name, description, computation type. |
30. | **Season Result** | Persisted, nightly-computed leaderboard standing per season/category. | Lookup to Season, lookup to Category, ranked entries (employee or poutine + score), computed-at timestamp. |
31. | **Hall of Fame Entry** | All-time winners, archived at season close. | Lookup to Season, lookup to Category, winner (employee or poutine), badge/title text. |

2. 
3. <!-- impeccable:product-schema 1 -->
4. 
5. ## Platform
6. 
7. web
8. 
9. ## Users
10. 
11. Employees of the company (~50 people, Montreal-based only), acting under their real employee identity (no anonymity). They use the app both on mobile (quick check-ins during breaks) and on desktop (at their workstation) in roughly equal measure — it must be fully responsive across both. This is the **employee-facing app only**; a separate admin/moderation app (out of scope for this document) serves the small (2–3 person) moderator group.
12. 
13. ## Product Purpose
14. 
15. The employee app is where colleagues submit poutines they've discovered at Montreal restaurants, browse/discover what others have found (list and map views), self-declare "tries," leave star ratings and written reviews, track seasonal and all-time leaderboards across four launch categories, and get help from an embedded conversational AI agent. Success means employees actually use it to connect socially over a shared love of poutine, while it also functions as a credible, polished showcase of AI-native Power Platform development.
16. 
17. ## Positioning
18. 
19. Not a generic review/rating app: it combines a confidence-weighted ("Bayesian-style") ranking that protects lightly-reviewed poutines from unfairly topping the board, a hard submission cap that rewards selectivity over volume, and agentic AI woven directly into core flows (duplicate detection at submission time, first-pass moderation, fun-fact generation, conversational assistance) rather than bolted on as a side feature.
20. 
21. ## Operating Context
22. 
23. - Runs as a Power Apps code app connected directly to Dataverse (single Dev environment, one unmanaged solution, for this demo).
24. - Real employee identity throughout — submissions, tries, and reviews are attributed to Dataverse system users (Entra ID-backed); no custom login/identity system.
25. - Embeds the interactive conversational agent (GitHub Copilot harness) as an in-app chat panel; the same agent is also published standalone to Microsoft 365 Copilot.
26. - Map view uses an open-source JS map library (e.g. Leaflet) centered on Montreal, with restaurant coordinates geocoded by a backend flow.
27. - Employee base is small (~50 people) — list, feed, and leaderboard density/pagination should assume a modest scale, not enterprise volume.
28. 
29. ## Capabilities and Constraints
30. 
31. - Submit a poutine (restaurant/place name + address, poutine name/description, price, photo, tags) — hard cap of **5 active submissions** per employee.
32. - New submissions go through lightweight AI-assisted first-pass moderation and a duplicate/similarity check before becoming publicly visible; ambiguous cases are escalated to human moderators via the separate admin app (not built here).
33. - "Trying" a poutine is self-declared (honor system, no proof required) and precedes leaving a review.
34. - A review is a star rating (1–5) plus a short written comment; reviews/ratings are visible to everyone, tied to the reviewer's real name.
35. - Discovery via a filterable list/feed (tags, neighborhood, rating) and a map view.
36. - Four launch leaderboard categories — Best Seller, Top Poutine (confidence-weighted rating), Best Supporter, Best Critic — tracked as both an all-time Hall of Fame and per-season (winter/spring/summer/autumn) standings.
37. - Notifications are intentionally minimal — season/category winner announcements only; day-to-day activity (someone trying your poutine, new reviews) is discovered by browsing, not pushed.
38. - Winner reward mechanics (symbolic vs. tangible) are explicitly **undecided** — do not assume or invent a reward beyond badges/titles/leaderboard recognition.
39. - No formal accessibility standard is mandated for this internal tool, but it should still follow solid, sensible accessibility practice.
40. - Fully responsive: must work well on both mobile and desktop, since employees use both roughly equally.
41. 
42. ## Brand Commitments
43. 
44. Inherits the shared "Comptoir Championship" visual system from `code-apps/DESIGN.md` (hand-painted casse-croûte aesthetic; fry-gold as the dominant color; ketchup-red reserved as a rare, meaningful accent). This app does not define its own visual identity — it consumes the shared design system.
45. 
46. ## Evidence on Hand
47. 
48. No real submissions, restaurant data, reviews, or brand assets exist yet. Sample/demo data is planned as versioned CSV/JSON seed files (restaurants, poutines, tags, reviews, seasons) loaded via the Dataverse skill's bulk-import capability. Do not fabricate real testimonials, reviews, or restaurant data beyond what is explicitly seeded.
49. 
50. ## Product Principles
51. 
52. - **Selectivity over volume.** Reward good taste and generosity in sharing it — never spam-submitting.
53. - **Fairness in rankings.** Confidence-weighted scoring protects lightly-reviewed entries from gaming the leaderboard.
54. - **AI woven in, not bolted on.** Duplicate detection, moderation assist, fun facts, and conversational help are core interactions, not side features.
55. - **Real identity, full transparency.** Every submission, try, and review is attributed to a real colleague.
56. - **Small-scale, high-craft.** ~50 users means density/scale assumptions stay modest; craft and delight matter more than raw scalability.
57. 
58. ## Accessibility & Inclusion
59. 
60. No formal standard (e.g. WCAG) is required for this internal tool; follow solid, sensible accessibility practice (semantic structure, keyboard operability, adequate contrast) as a baseline expectation.

2. name: app-implementation
3. description: >
4.   Orchestrates Power Apps Code App work in a Power Platform project using the
5.   `code-apps-preview` plugin (microsoft/power-platform-skills).   Use when working on any task involving
6.   Power Apps code apps: scaffolding new apps, connecting data sources, adding connectors,
7.   and deploying. Triggers on: create code app, add data source, add connector, deploy app,
8.   connect Dataverse/SharePoint/Teams/Excel/OneDrive/Office365/Azure DevOps to app.
9.   Do NOT use for Copilot Studio agents (use agent-implementation), Power Automate flows
10.   (use backend-process-implementation), or Dataverse schema work alone (use data-management).
11. ---
12. 
13. # app-implementation
14. 
15. Orchestration layer for all Power Apps Code App work in this project.
16. The `code-apps-preview` plugin provides the full scaffold-to-deploy lifecycle.
17. 
18. ## Step 0 — Dependency preflight (required)
19. 
20. Before routing any app task, verify `code-apps-preview` sub-skills are available:
21. `create-code-app`, `add-dataverse`, `add-sharepoint`, `add-excel`, `add-onedrive`,
22. `add-teams`, `add-office365`, `add-azuredevops`, `add-connector`, `add-datasource`,
23. and `deploy`.
24. 
25. If any required sub-skill is missing or unavailable:
26. 1. Stop execution and return a blocked status.
27. 2. Ask the user whether they want to install or enable the missing dependency.
28. 3. Resume only after availability is confirmed.
29. 
30. Do not handcraft connector scaffolding or generated bindings as a fallback for missing skills.
31. 
32. ## Step 1 — Environment and solution scope gate (required)
33. 
34. Before any code-app work starts, require explicit target scope:
35. - Environment: display name and environment ID (or URL)
36. - Solution: unique name and publisher prefix for the solution that will contain app assets
37. 
38. If either environment or solution is missing, ambiguous, or inferred:
39. 1. Stop execution and return a blocked status.
40. 2. Ask the user to explicitly provide the target environment and solution.
41. 3. Resume only after both are confirmed.
42. 
43. Do not scaffold, connect data sources, or deploy against an implicit target.
44. 
45. ## Step 2 — Design alignment with Impeccable (strongly recommended)
46. 
47. Power Apps code apps are React apps. Run the `impeccable` skill to establish and maintain
48. design quality throughout the full lifecycle, not just at init.
49. 
50. ### Shared DESIGN.md + per-app PRODUCT.md pattern
51. 
52. This is natively supported by Impeccable's monorepo path resolution:
53. 
54. - **Shared `DESIGN.md`** — lives at `code-apps/DESIGN.md`. One design system, all apps.
55.   **This already exists for Poutine League** (the "Comptoir Championship" system) — `impeccable
56.   document` is a one-time step, already done; do not regenerate it without an explicit request
57.   and human approval.
58. - **Shared `.impeccable/`** — lives at `code-apps/` with a `config.json` declaring each
59.   `code-apps/<app-name>` as a `projectRoot`. This tells Impeccable to walk up and find the
60.   shared DESIGN.md when running inside any app subfolder.
61. - **Per-app `PRODUCT.md`** — lives at `code-apps/<app-name>/PRODUCT.md`. Product context
62.   (users, purpose, brand personality, constraints) is specific to each app. Do not confuse this
63.   with the root-level `PRODUCT.md` (whole-product functional vision) — see root `AGENTS.md`.
64. 
65. **One-time setup (before first code app):** run `impeccable document` at `code-apps/` to
66. generate the shared `DESIGN.md`. This captures the design system that all apps in the project
67. will inherit. If no code exists yet, use `impeccable new-work` to establish the visual world
68. from scratch. Do not scaffold or build any code app before this step.
69. 
70. **Per-app setup (before each new code app):** run `impeccable init --target code-apps/<app-name>/`
71. to write the app's `PRODUCT.md`. This interview pins product context (users, purpose, brand
72. personality, constraints) to the app before any code is written. Root `PRODUCT.md` (and, for
73. agent context, `ARCHITECTURE.md` §5) already identify the two expected apps — **employee app**
74. and **admin/moderation app** — use them to seed this interview rather than starting from scratch.
75. 
76. Impeccable resolves the shared `DESIGN.md` automatically via the `config.json` `projectRoots`
77. when running inside any app subfolder.
78. 
79. ### Design artifact governance
80. 
81. `DESIGN.md`, `PRODUCT.md`, and `.impeccable/` files are human-owned. Do not write or modify
82. them autonomously during a working session.
83. 
84. When the agent identifies that an update would improve accuracy (e.g., new design tokens
85. introduced, product scope shifted, a component was added):
86. 
87. 1. **Formulate the proposed change**: describe what would change and why.
88. 2. **Present it to the user** and wait for explicit approval.
89. 3. **Apply only if approved**. If declined, note the divergence and continue.
90. 
91. This applies to every write — including minor corrections, token additions, and regeneration
92. via `document` or `init`. Never invoke these commands autonomously.
93. 
94. ### Impeccable lifecycle for code apps
95. 
96. | Phase | Command | When to use |
97. |-------|---------|-------------|
98. | **Before first app** | `document` | **Strongly recommended**: generates shared `code-apps/DESIGN.md` from existing code (or `new-work` if no code yet) |
99. | **Before each new app** | `init` | **Strongly recommended**: per-app PRODUCT.md — pins users, purpose, brand, constraints |
100. | **Before building** | `shape [feature]` | Plan UX/UI before writing code; runs a discovery interview and produces a design brief |
101. | **During development** | `hooks on` | Activates design detector — fires after every file edit and flags anti-patterns |
102. | **During development** | `live` | Interactive browser variant mode — pick elements, generate alternatives in real time |
103. | **Evaluate (pre-PR)** | `critique [target]` | UX review: visual hierarchy, IA, cognitive load, heuristic scoring |
104. | **Evaluate (pre-PR)** | `audit [target]` | Technical quality: a11y (WCAG), perf, responsive, anti-patterns (P0-P3 severity) |
105. | **Refine** | `polish [target]` | Final quality pass: alignment, spacing, consistency, micro-details |
106. | **Refine** | `harden [target]` | Production-ready: error states, i18n, text overflow, edge cases |
107. | **Refine** | `onboard [target]` | First-run flows, empty states, activation moments |
108. | **Targeted fix** | `adapt [target]` | Responsive and multi-device adaptation |
109. | **Targeted fix** | `layout [target]` | Spacing, rhythm, visual hierarchy |
110. | **Targeted fix** | `clarify [target]` | UX copy, labels, error messages |
111. | **Targeted fix** | `typeset [target]` | Typography hierarchy and font choices |
112. | **Targeted fix** | `optimize [target]` | UI performance: loading, rendering, bundle size |
113. | **Enhance** | `colorize / animate / delight` | Strategic color, motion, personality |
114. | **Maintenance** | `doctor` | Detects and repairs drift between PRODUCT.md, DESIGN.md, and .impeccable/ artifacts |
115. 
116. **Mandatory gates for new apps:** `document` (if first app or no DESIGN.md) → `init` → `shape` → `hooks on`
117. 
118. **Pre-PR gates:** `critique` + `audit` before opening a pull request. Surface Critical/High findings to the user.
119. 
120. If the user explicitly skips `document` or `init`, proceed but record the gap and surface it at
121. review time. Never disable or silently ignore design hook findings.
122. 
123. If the `impeccable` skill is unavailable, flag the gap and do not attempt to reproduce its
124. behaviour manually.
125. 
126. ## Available sub-skills
127. 
128. | Sub-skill | When to use |
129. |-----------|-------------|
130. | `create-code-app` | Start any new app — always the first step |
131. | `add-dataverse` | Connect a Dataverse table as a data source |
132. | `add-sharepoint` | Connect a SharePoint list or library |
133. | `add-excel` | Connect an Excel workbook |
134. | `add-onedrive` | Connect OneDrive files |
135. | `add-teams` | Connect Microsoft Teams data |
136. | `add-office365` | Connect Outlook, Calendar, or other O365 data |
137. | `add-azuredevops` | Connect Azure DevOps work items or repos |
138. | `add-connector` | Add any other connector (premium or standard) |
139. | `add-datasource` | Use when the right connector is unclear — it resolves the best fit |
140. | `deploy` | Push the app to the Power Platform environment |
141. 
142. ## Project conventions
143. 
144. ### App folder structure
145. All code apps live under `code-apps/<app-name>/` at the repo root.
146. Never create app files outside this path.
147. 
148. ### Preferred data source
149. Prefer Dataverse as the primary data source.
150. - New app with data needs → `add-dataverse` unless there is an explicit reason not to.
151. - Unclear source → `add-datasource` (it selects the best connector).
152. - Non-Dataverse sources are valid when the data lives there natively (SharePoint lists,
153.   Excel workbooks, etc.).
154. 
155. ### Generated files are read-only
156. Never edit files under `src/generated/` by hand.
157. These files are regenerated automatically when connector sub-skills run.
158. Hand edits will be overwritten and may corrupt the connector binding.
159. 
160. ### Pre-push quality gates (Makefile contract)
161. Use gate targets to keep terminology aligned across app and solution work:
162. 
163. - `app-gate` = `app-lint` + `app-test`
164. - `solution-gate` = `solution-pack` + `solution-check`
165. 
166. Before calling `deploy` or running `pac code push`:
167. 1. `make app-gate` — mandatory for code-app changes.
168. 2. `make build` — optional confidence gate.
169. 3. `make solution-gate` — required when solution artifacts change.
170. 
171. If any required gate fails, fix errors before deploying.
172. 
173. ### Premium connector confirmation
174. Before adding any premium connector via `add-connector`:
175. 1. Identify the connector tier (premium vs. standard).
176. 2. Surface the DLP policy implications to the user.
177. 3. **Wait for explicit human confirmation** before executing `add-connector`.
178. 
179. This applies even in autopilot mode. Premium connectors affect licensing and DLP — the
180. human must acknowledge before the connector is added.
181. 
182. ## Standard workflow
183. 
184. ```
185. New app
186.   └─ Dependency preflight
187.        ├─ Missing dependency? → ask to install/enable → stop until resolved
188.        └─ Scope gate (environment + solution explicit)
189.             ├─ Missing or ambiguous? → ask user → stop until resolved
190.             └─ DESIGN.md exists at code-apps/?
191.                  ├─ No → strongly recommend: impeccable document (or new-work) → wait for human approval before writing
192.                  └─ Yes (or approved) → impeccable init (per-app PRODUCT.md) → wait for human approval before writing
193.                       └─ shape → hooks on → create-code-app
194.                            └─ add-dataverse (default) or add-datasource (unclear source)
195.                                 └─ [optional] add additional sources
196.                                      └─ impeccable: critique + audit (pre-PR gates)
197.                                           └─ make app-gate
198.                                                └─ [optional] make build
199.                                                     └─ [if solution changed] make solution-gate
200.                                                          └─ deploy
201. ```
202. 
203. ```
204. Modify existing app
205.   └─ Dependency preflight
206.        ├─ Missing dependency? → ask to install/enable → stop until resolved
207.        └─ Scope gate (environment + solution explicit)
208.             ├─ Missing or ambiguous? → ask user → stop until resolved
209.             └─ Design context (impeccable context — if PRODUCT.md/DESIGN.md exist)
210.                  └─ Identify change type
211.                       ├─ New data source → appropriate add-* sub-skill
212.                       │    └─ Premium? → flag DLP + confirm → add-connector
213.                       └─ No new source → edit, then make app-gate
214.                            └─ [optional] make build
215.                                 └─ [if solution changed] make solution-gate
216.                                      └─ deploy
217. ```
218. 
219. ## Escape hatches
220. 
221. - If `create-code-app` fails due to environment targeting, run `route-environments` from
222.   the `power-automate` plugin to verify the active environment, then retry.
223. - If `deploy` fails with a DLP error, surface the full error message to the user and pause
224.   for guidance rather than retrying automatically.
225. - If the `impeccable` skill is unavailable, proceed without the design preflight but flag
226.   the gap — do not silently skip and do not attempt to reproduce Impeccable's behaviour
227.   manually.

98. # Design System: Poutine League
99. 
100. ## Overview
101. 
102. **Creative North Star: "The Comptoir Championship"**
103. 
104. Poutine League looks like the laminated menu board and hand-painted sign above a beloved Montreal casse-croûte — warm, confident, a little cheeky, built to be read at a glance from the counter. The system takes its cues from comptoir culture: chalkboard specials, sticker-badged loyalty cards, laminated table numbers, and the taped-up "Champion of the Month" photo by the register. It exists to make an internal work tool feel like a neighborhood ritual, not a dashboard.
105. 
106. Flat and graphic, never soft or glassy: surfaces separate with ink-black outlines and hard offset shadows like laminated cardstock, not blurred drop shadows. Fry-gold is the one color every screen is built around; ketchup-red is reserved and only appears where it means something (a call to action, a live rating, an alert). Rejected explicitly: cold blues/grays, glassmorphism, soft blurred shadows, gradient mesh backgrounds, and generic rounded-icon-tile chrome — none of it belongs in a casse-croûte.
107. 
108. The admin/moderation app inherits the same palette, type, and shape language, but its composition is calmer and denser — a back-of-house control panel run by the same counter, not a second brand.
109. 
110. **Key Characteristics:**
111. - Hand-painted sign-board display type paired with a clean workhorse body face for scanability.
112. - One dominant saturated color (fry-gold) per screen; ketchup-red stays rare and meaningful.
113. - Flat surfaces, ink-black borders, hard offset "sticker" shadows — no blur, no glass.
114. - Checkerboard motif used sparingly as a divider/accent, never as a busy full background.
115. - Pill-shaped chips and badges everywhere small facts (tags, ranks, status) need to be scanned fast.
116. 
117. ## Colors
118. 
119. A warm, committed palette: fry-gold carries the surface, ketchup-red is the rare exclamation mark, and everything else sits in creamy counter-neutrals.
120. 
121. ### Primary
122. - **Fry Gold** (`#D99A2B`): the system's dominant color — primary buttons, active nav state, header bands, hero sections, the "one griddle" every screen is built around.
123. - **Fry Gold Deep** (`#B87A1C`): hover/active/pressed state for fry-gold surfaces.
124. 
125. ### Secondary
126. - **Ketchup Red** (`#C23B2E`): reserved for meaning, not decoration — primary CTAs that commit an action (submit, approve), live star ratings, and destructive/alert states.
127. - **Ketchup Red Deep** (`#9C2B21`): hover/active state for ketchup-red surfaces.
128. 
129. ### Tertiary
130. - **Relish Green** (`#5C7A3A`): approved/success states only (submission approved, connection healthy).
131. - **Mustard Amber** (`#E0A419`): pending/in-review states only (submission in moderation, season in progress).
132. 
133. ### Neutral
134. - **Cream Counter** (`#FBF3E6`): page background — the laminate-countertop base, never stark white.
135. - **Paper White** (`#FFFDF8`): card/surface background, one step lighter than the page for gentle separation.
136. - **Checker Light** (`#EDD9B8`): tag chips, table zebra-striping, and the checkerboard accent motif.
137. - **Gravy Ink** (`#2A1D14`): borders and outlines — the "hand-painted line" that separates every surface.
138. - **Gravy Text** (`#3A2A1E`): primary body/heading text color.
139. - **Gravy Text Soft** (`#6B5644`): secondary/meta text (timestamps, helper copy, counts).
140. 
141. ### Named Rules
142. **The One Griddle Rule.** Fry-gold owns exactly one dominant region per screen — a header band, a hero card, or the primary CTA — never more than one at a time. Spend it once per screen or it stops feeling special.
143. 
144. **The Ketchup Is Punctuation Rule.** Ketchup-red never fills a background or a large region. It marks the single thing on a screen that wants a reaction: submit, approve, a 5-star badge, a "your turn" alert.
145. 
146. ## Typography
147. 
148. **Display Font:** Alfa Slab One (with Georgia, serif fallback)
149. **Body Font:** Inter (with system-ui, sans-serif fallback)
150. **Label/Score Font:** ui-monospace stack (SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Consolas)
151. 
152. **Character:** Alfa Slab One brings the thick, confident stroke of a hand-painted menu board to hero moments and section titles; Inter stays out of the way for everything an employee actually has to read and act on. The monospace score face gives ranks, ratings, and prices the tabular precision of a scoreboard.
153. 
154. ### Hierarchy
155. - **Display** (400, `clamp(2.25rem, 5vw, 3.75rem)`, 1.05): page heroes, season-winner announcements, empty-state headlines.
156. - **Headline** (400, `clamp(1.5rem, 3vw, 2.25rem)`, 1.1): section titles ("Leaderboard", "Review Queue"), card group headers.
157. - **Title** (700, 1.25rem, 1.3): card titles (poutine name, restaurant name), button labels.
158. - **Body** (400, 1rem, 1.5): reviews, descriptions, form fields. Wrap at 65–75ch for reviews and comments.
159. - **Label** (600, 0.8125rem, 1.2, 0.02em tracking): tag chips, status badges, table headers — uppercase where used as a category marker.
160. - **Score** (700, 1.125rem, 1, mono, tabular): star ratings, leaderboard ranks, prices, review counts.
161. 
162. ### Named Rules
163. **The Menu Board Rule.** Alfa Slab One is for moments that deserve a beat — hero, headline, a crowned winner. It never appears in body copy, form labels, or dense admin tables; there it steps aside for Inter.
164. 
165. ## Layout
166. 
167. A single comfortable content column (max 1200px) with generous top-of-section spacing over bottom, matching the spacing scale (4/8/16/24/40px). Employee app screens breathe — cards have room, the map/list toggle sits prominently, leaderboards use full-width rank rows. The admin app tightens the same rhythm: denser tables, smaller card padding (use `sm`/`md` spacing over `lg`/`xl`), more rows visible per screen, because its 2–3 users optimize for throughput over atmosphere. Both apps share the same 12px grid baseline and the same breakpoint behavior: single column below 640px, two-column card grids from 640–1024px, full multi-column leaderboard/table layouts above 1024px.
168. 
169. ## Elevation & Depth
170. 
171. Flat by design, with depth conveyed through ink-black outlines and hard, unblurred offset shadows — like laminated cardstock stacked on a counter, never glass or soft ambient light. Nothing in this system uses `blur()`, gradient meshes, or floating glass panels.
172. 
173. ### Shadow Vocabulary
174. - **Sticker** (`box-shadow: 3px 3px 0 #2A1D14`): default resting shadow for cards, buttons, and badges — a hard, single-direction offset with zero blur.
175. - **Sticker Pressed** (`box-shadow: 1px 1px 0 #2A1D14`): active/pressed state, shadow compresses as the element "sits down" on the counter.
176. - **Sticker Lifted** (`box-shadow: 5px 5px 0 #2A1D14`): hover state on interactive cards, shadow grows slightly as if peeling up off the counter.
177. 
178. ### Named Rules
179. **The Laminate Rule.** Depth comes from a hard offset shadow and a visible ink border, never from blur. If a surface needs to look "elevated," give it more offset — not more blur.
180. 
181. ## Shapes
182. 
183. Borders are the load-bearing visual device: every card, button, and chip carries a 2px `gravy-ink` outline, echoing a hand-painted sign's confident line. Corners are generously rounded — `sm` (6px) for tight controls, `md` (12px) for cards, `lg` (20px) for hero/feature cards — evoking laminated menu cards and rounded diner signage rather than sharp corporate rectangles. Interactive chips, badges, and primary/secondary buttons are full pills (`999px`), like loyalty-card stamps or rank medals. The checkerboard motif (alternating `cream-counter`/`checker-light` squares) appears only as a thin divider strip or footer/header band accent — never as a full-page background, where it would overwhelm content.
184. 
185. ## Components
186. 
187. ### Buttons
188. - **Shape:** full pill (`999px` radius), 2px `gravy-ink` border, Sticker shadow at rest.
189. - **Primary:** `fry-gold` background, `gravy-ink` text, Title typography, 12px/28px padding. Reserved for the one primary action per screen (Submit, Approve).
190. - **Secondary:** `paper-white` background, `gravy-ink` text and border, same shape/padding — used for all non-primary actions.
191. - **Destructive/Alert:** same shape, `ketchup-red` background, `paper-white` text — reject, delete, cancel actions only.
192. - **Hover / Focus:** background shifts to the `-deep` variant; shadow grows to Sticker Lifted; focus ring is a 3px `gravy-ink` outline offset 2px, never a soft glow.
193. 
194. ### Chips (tags, status)
195. - **Style:** `checker-light` background, `gravy-text` label type, full pill, no border (chips are quieter than cards/buttons).
196. - **State:** status chips swap fill color by meaning — `mustard-amber` for in-review, `relish-green` for approved, `ketchup-red` for rejected — always paired with a text label, never color alone.
197. 
198. ### Cards / Containers
199. - **Corner Style:** `md` (12px) for poutine/review cards, `lg` (20px) for hero/leaderboard-winner cards.
200. - **Border/Shadow:** 2px `gravy-ink` border + Sticker shadow at rest, Sticker Lifted on hover for anything clickable.
201. - **Content Rhythm:** image/photo first (poutine photo), Title below, meta row (rating score, tag chips) beneath that, using `sm`–`md` internal spacing.
202. 
203. ### Leaderboard / Rank Badges
204. - **Shape:** circular, 40px, `fry-gold` fill, `gravy-ink` border, Score typography centered.
205. - **Top-1 treatment:** the current season/all-time #1 gets a `mustard-amber` ring accent outside the badge border — the closest this system gets to a literal medal, used sparingly (only true #1 placements, never generic "featured" tagging).
206. 
207. ### Map & List Views (Employee app discovery)
208. - **List rows:** card treatment above, one row per poutine, rank/score right-aligned in Score typography.
209. - **Map pins:** circular `fry-gold`-filled pins with `gravy-ink` border matching the rank-badge shape language, so map and list feel like one system, not two.
210. 
211. ## Do's and Don'ts
212. 
213. **Do:**
214. - Spend fry-gold once per screen as the dominant region (header, hero, or primary CTA).
215. - Keep every border `gravy-ink`, every shadow hard-offset with zero blur.
216. - Use the checkerboard motif only as a thin accent strip, never a full background.
217. - Give the admin app the same palette and shapes, just tighter spacing and smaller type scale usage.
218. - Pair every status color with a text label — never rely on color alone for meaning.
219. 
220. **Don't:**
221. - Don't use soft blurred shadows, glassmorphism, or gradient-mesh backgrounds — this system is flat and hard-edged by doctrine.
222. - Don't let ketchup-red fill a background, nav bar, or large region — it's punctuation, not paint.
223. - Don't introduce cool blues/grays or stock "SaaS" gradient icon tiles — everything visual should feel hand-made for a casse-croûte, not a generic dashboard template.
224. - Don't use Alfa Slab One for body copy, table cells, or form labels — reserve it for hero/headline moments only.
225. - Don't stack more than one rounded-radius scale on the same element family (e.g., don't mix `md` and `lg` cards in the same grid).

# Use OData to query data

Every query starts with a collection of entities. Entity collections include:

- EntitySet resources: One of the Web API `EntitySet` collections.
- Filtered collections: A set of entities returned by a [collection-valued navigation property](../web-api-navigation-properties#collection-valued-navigation-properties) for a specific record.
- [An expanded collection-valued navigation property](join-tables#expand-collection-valued-navigation-properties).
- [A collection returned by a function](../use-web-api-functions#composable-functions).

## `EntitySet` resources

To find all the `EntitySet` resources available in your environment, send a `GET` request to the Web API [service document](../web-api-service-documents#service-document):

**Request:**

```http
GET [Organization URI]/api/data/v9.2/
Accept: application/json  
OData-MaxVersion: 4.0  
OData-Version: 4.0
```

**Response:**

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK  
Content-Type: application/json; odata.metadata=minimal  
OData-Version: 4.0  

{
    "@odata.context": "[Organization URI]/api/data/v9.2/$metadata",
    "value": [
        {
            "name": "aadusers",
            "kind": "EntitySet",
            "url": "aadusers"
        },
        {
            "name": "accountleadscollection",
            "kind": "EntitySet",
            "url": "accountleadscollection"
        },
        {
            "name": "accounts",
            "kind": "EntitySet",
            "url": "accounts"
        },
      ... <Truncated for brevity>
   [
}
```

Tip

These values are usually the plural name of the table, but they can be different. Use the results of this request to confirm you're using the correct `EntitySet` resource name.

For example, start with the `accounts` EntitySet resource to retrieve data from the [account entity type](/en-us/power-apps/developer/data-platform/webapi/reference/account).

```http
GET [Organization URI]/api/data/v9.2/accounts
```

## Filtered collections

You can query any collection of entities that a collection-valued navigation property represents for a specified record. For example, if you want to retrieve data from the [account entity type](/en-us/power-apps/developer/data-platform/webapi/reference/account) where a specific user is the [OwningUser](../../reference/entities/account#BKMK_OwningUser), use the `user_accounts` collection-valued navigation property from the specified [systemuser](/en-us/power-apps/developer/data-platform/webapi/reference/systemuser) record.

```http
GET [Organization URI]/api/data/v9.2/systemusers(<systemuserid value>)/user_accounts?$select=name
```

To find the name of the collection-valued navigation property:

- For any Dataverse tables and relationships, check the [Web API Entity Type Reference](/en-us/power-apps/developer/data-platform/webapi/reference/entitytypes).
- For any custom tables or relationships, look for the [collection-valued navigation properties](../web-api-navigation-properties#collection-valued-navigation-properties) within the [$metadata service document](../web-api-service-documents#csdl-metadata-document).

## Retrieve data

To retrieve data from a collection, send a `GET` request to the collection resource. The following example shows retrieving data from the [account entity type](/en-us/power-apps/developer/data-platform/webapi/reference/account).

This example also demonstrates:

- Limiting the columns returned by using `$select`. [Learn more about selecting columns](select-columns).
- Ordering results by using `$orderby`. [Learn more about ordering columns](order-rows).
- Limiting the rows returned by using `$top`. Learn about limiting the number of rows.
- Showing formatted values by using the request header: `Prefer: odata.include-annotations="OData.Community.Display.V1.FormattedValue"`. [Learn about formatted values](select-columns#formatted-values).

**Request:**

```http
GET [Organization URI]/api/data/v9.2/accounts?$select=name,statecode,statuscode&$orderby=name&$top=1
Accept: application/json  
OData-MaxVersion: 4.0  
OData-Version: 4.0
Prefer: odata.include-annotations="OData.Community.Display.V1.FormattedValue"
```

**Response:**

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK  
Content-Type: application/json; odata.metadata=minimal  
OData-Version: 4.0  
Preference-Applied: odata.include-annotations="OData.Community.Display.V1.FormattedValue"

{
   "@odata.context": "[Organization URI]/api/data/v9.2/$metadata#accounts(name,statecode,statuscode)",
   "value": [

         "name": "A. Datum Corporation (sample)",

         "statecode": 0,
         "statuscode@OData.Community.Display.V1.FormattedValue": "Active",

}
```

## Refine your query

After you select the table to start your query, refine the query to get the data you need. The following articles explain how to complete your query.

| Article | Task |
| --- | --- |
| [Select columns](select-columns) | Specify which columns of data to return. |
| [Join tables](join-tables) | Specify which related tables to return in the results. |
| [Order rows](order-rows) | Specify the sort order of the rows to return. |
| [Filter rows](filter-rows) | Specify which rows of data to return. |
| [Page results](page-results) | Specify how many rows of data to return with each request. |
| [Aggregate data](aggregate-data) | How to group and aggregate the data returned. |
| [Count number of rows](count-rows) | How to get a count of the number of rows returned. |
| [Performance optimizations](optimize-performance) | How to optimize performance. |

## OData query options

Use these options to change the results returned from a collection. The following table describes the OData query options the Dataverse Web API supports.

| Option | Use to | More information |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `$select` | Request a specific set of properties for each entity or complex type. | [Select columns](select-columns) |
| `$expand` | Specify the related resources to include in line with retrieved resources. | [Join tables](join-tables) |
| `$orderby` | Request resources in a particular order. | [Order rows](order-rows) |
| `$filter` | Filter a collection of resources. | [Filter rows](filter-rows) |
| `$apply` | Aggregate and group your data. | [Aggregate data](aggregate-data) |
| `$top` | Specify the number of items in the queried collection to include in the result. | Limit the number of rows |
| `$count` | Request a count of the matching resources to include with the resources in the response. | [Count number of rows](count-rows) |

To apply multiple options, separate query options from the resource path with a question mark (`?`). Separate each option after the first with an ampersand (`&`). Option names are case-sensitive.

### Use parameter aliases with query options

You can use parameter aliases for `$filter` and `$orderby` query options, but not inside the `$expand` option. Parameter aliases allow you to use the same value multiple times in a request. If the alias doesn't have an assigned value, it's null.

Without parameter aliases:

```http
GET [Organization URI]/api/data/v9.2/accounts?$select=name,revenue
&$orderby=revenue asc,name desc
&$filter=revenue ne null
```

With parameter aliases:

```http
GET [Organization URI]/api/data/v9.2/accounts?$select=name,revenue
&$orderby=@p1 asc,@p2 desc
&$filter=@p1 ne @p3&@p1=revenue&@p2=name
```

You can also use parameter aliases when using functions. [Learn to use Web API functions](../use-web-api-functions)

### Unsupported OData query options

The Dataverse Web API doesn't support the following [OData query options](https://docs.oasis-open.org/odata/odata/v4.0/errata03/os/complete/part2-url-conventions/odata-v4.0-errata03-os-part2-url-conventions-complete.html#_Toc453752356): `$skip`, `$search`, and `$format`.

### URL length limitations

The length of a URL in a `GET` request [is limited to 32 KB (32,768 characters)](../compose-http-requests-handle-errors#maximum-url-length). Including many complex OData query options as a parameter in the URL can reach the limit. You can execute a `$batch` operation by using a `POST` request as a way to move the OData query options out of the URL and into the body of the request where the limit is twice as long. By sending a `GET` request within a `$batch`, you can use URLs up to 64 KB (65,536 characters) in length. [Learn more about batch operations using the Web API](../execute-batch-operations-using-web-api).

## Limit the number of rows

To limit the number of rows returned, use the `$top` OData query option. Without this limit, Dataverse returns up to 5,000 standard table rows and 500 elastic table rows.

Alternatively, specify a number of records to return by using paging. Don't use `$top` when you request pages of data. [Learn how to request paged results](page-results).

## Limitations

There are some things that you can do by using FetchXml that OData doesn't support.

- You can't [join tables without any relationship](../../fetchxml/join-tables#no-relationship). OData only allows using the `$expand` query option to join tables by using navigation properties that are part of the relationships in the data model.
- [You can't use nested $expand with N:N relationships](join-tables#nested-expand-with-nn-relationships).
- [Aggregation limitations](aggregate-data#odata-aggregation-limitations) lists the following limitations for aggregations by using OData:

    - [Get distinct number with CountColumn](aggregate-data#get-distinct-number-with-countcolumn)
    - [Time zone when grouping by date](aggregate-data#time-zone-when-grouping-by-date)
    - [Row aggregate](aggregate-data#row-aggregate)
    - [Per query limit](aggregate-data#per-query-limit)
- [Perform cross table column comparisons](../../fetchxml/filter-rows#cross-table-column-comparisons). OData supports [filtering on column values in the same row](filter-rows#column-comparison), but they must be in the same table.
- [You don't need to override the default sort order for choice columns](../../fetchxml/order-rows#override-default-choice-columns-sort-order). The default behavior when sorting choice columns is to use the integer values rather than the localized label value.
- You can't use the [Late Materialize query](../../fetchxml/optimize-performance#late-materialize-query) performance optimization.

Note

Microsoft doesn't support tools created by the community. If you have questions or problems with community tools, contact the publisher of the tool.

# Design System: Poutine League

## Overview

**Creative North Star: "The Comptoir Championship"**

Poutine League looks like the laminated menu board and hand-painted sign above a beloved Montreal casse-croûte — warm, confident, a little cheeky, built to be read at a glance from the counter. The system takes its cues from comptoir culture: chalkboard specials, sticker-badged loyalty cards, laminated table numbers, and the taped-up "Champion of the Month" photo by the register. It exists to make an internal work tool feel like a neighborhood ritual, not a dashboard.

Flat and graphic, never soft or glassy: surfaces separate with ink-black outlines and hard offset shadows like laminated cardstock, not blurred drop shadows. Fry-gold is the one color every screen is built around; ketchup-red is reserved and only appears where it means something (a call to action, a live rating, an alert). Rejected explicitly: cold blues/grays, glassmorphism, soft blurred shadows, gradient mesh backgrounds, and generic rounded-icon-tile chrome — none of it belongs in a casse-croûte.

The admin/moderation app inherits the same palette, type, and shape language, but its composition is calmer and denser — a back-of-house control panel run by the same counter, not a second brand.

**Key Characteristics:**
- Hand-painted sign-board display type paired with a clean workhorse body face for scanability.
- One dominant saturated color (fry-gold) per screen; ketchup-red stays rare and meaningful.
- Flat surfaces, ink-black borders, hard offset "sticker" shadows — no blur, no glass.
- Checkerboard motif used sparingly as a divider/accent, never as a busy full background.
- Pill-shaped chips and badges everywhere small facts (tags, ranks, status) need to be scanned fast.

## Colors

A warm, committed palette: fry-gold carries the surface, ketchup-red is the rare exclamation mark, and everything else sits in creamy counter-neutrals.

### Primary
- **Fry Gold** (`#D99A2B`): the system's dominant color — primary buttons, active nav state, header bands, hero sections, the "one griddle" every screen is built around.
- **Fry Gold Deep** (`#B87A1C`): hover/active/pressed state for fry-gold surfaces.

### Secondary
- **Ketchup Red** (`#C23B2E`): reserved for meaning, not decoration — primary CTAs that commit an action (submit, approve), live star ratings, and destructive/alert states.
- **Ketchup Red Deep** (`#9C2B21`): hover/active state for ketchup-red surfaces.

### Tertiary
- **Relish Green** (`#5C7A3A`): approved/success states only (submission approved, connection healthy).
- **Mustard Amber** (`#E0A419`): pending/in-review states only (submission in moderation, season in progress).

### Neutral
- **Cream Counter** (`#FBF3E6`): page background — the laminate-countertop base, never stark white.
- **Paper White** (`#FFFDF8`): card/surface background, one step lighter than the page for gentle separation.
- **Checker Light** (`#EDD9B8`): tag chips, table zebra-striping, and the checkerboard accent motif.
- **Gravy Ink** (`#2A1D14`): borders and outlines — the "hand-painted line" that separates every surface.
- **Gravy Text** (`#3A2A1E`): primary body/heading text color.
- **Gravy Text Soft** (`#6B5644`): secondary/meta text (timestamps, helper copy, counts).

### Named Rules
**The One Griddle Rule.** Fry-gold owns exactly one dominant region per screen — a header band, a hero card, or the primary CTA — never more than one at a time. Spend it once per screen or it stops feeling special.

**The Ketchup Is Punctuation Rule.** Ketchup-red never fills a background or a large region. It marks the single thing on a screen that wants a reaction: submit, approve, a 5-star badge, a "your turn" alert.

## Typography

**Display Font:** Alfa Slab One (with Georgia, serif fallback)
**Body Font:** Inter (with system-ui, sans-serif fallback)
**Label/Score Font:** ui-monospace stack (SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Consolas)

**Character:** Alfa Slab One brings the thick, confident stroke of a hand-painted menu board to hero moments and section titles; Inter stays out of the way for everything an employee actually has to read and act on. The monospace score face gives ranks, ratings, and prices the tabular precision of a scoreboard.

### Hierarchy
- **Display** (400, `clamp(2.25rem, 5vw, 3.75rem)`, 1.05): page heroes, season-winner announcements, empty-state headlines.
- **Headline** (400, `clamp(1.5rem, 3vw, 2.25rem)`, 1.1): section titles ("Leaderboard", "Review Queue"), card group headers.
- **Title** (700, 1.25rem, 1.3): card titles (poutine name, restaurant name), button labels.
- **Body** (400, 1rem, 1.5): reviews, descriptions, form fields. Wrap at 65–75ch for reviews and comments.
- **Label** (600, 0.8125rem, 1.2, 0.02em tracking): tag chips, status badges, table headers — uppercase where used as a category marker.
- **Score** (700, 1.125rem, 1, mono, tabular): star ratings, leaderboard ranks, prices, review counts.

### Named Rules
**The Menu Board Rule.** Alfa Slab One is for moments that deserve a beat — hero, headline, a crowned winner. It never appears in body copy, form labels, or dense admin tables; there it steps aside for Inter.

## Layout

A single comfortable content column (max 1200px) with generous top-of-section spacing over bottom, matching the spacing scale (4/8/16/24/40px). Employee app screens breathe — cards have room, the map/list toggle sits prominently, leaderboards use full-width rank rows. The admin app tightens the same rhythm: denser tables, smaller card padding (use `sm`/`md` spacing over `lg`/`xl`), more rows visible per screen, because its 2–3 users optimize for throughput over atmosphere. Both apps share the same 12px grid baseline and the same breakpoint behavior: single column below 640px, two-column card grids from 640–1024px, full multi-column leaderboard/table layouts above 1024px.

## Elevation & Depth

Flat by design, with depth conveyed through ink-black outlines and hard, unblurred offset shadows — like laminated cardstock stacked on a counter, never glass or soft ambient light. Nothing in this system uses `blur()`, gradient meshes, or floating glass panels.

### Shadow Vocabulary
- **Sticker** (`box-shadow: 3px 3px 0 #2A1D14`): default resting shadow for cards, buttons, and badges — a hard, single-direction offset with zero blur.
- **Sticker Pressed** (`box-shadow: 1px 1px 0 #2A1D14`): active/pressed state, shadow compresses as the element "sits down" on the counter.
- **Sticker Lifted** (`box-shadow: 5px 5px 0 #2A1D14`): hover state on interactive cards, shadow grows slightly as if peeling up off the counter.

### Named Rules
**The Laminate Rule.** Depth comes from a hard offset shadow and a visible ink border, never from blur. If a surface needs to look "elevated," give it more offset — not more blur.

## Shapes

Borders are the load-bearing visual device: every card, button, and chip carries a 2px `gravy-ink` outline, echoing a hand-painted sign's confident line. Corners are generously rounded — `sm` (6px) for tight controls, `md` (12px) for cards, `lg` (20px) for hero/feature cards — evoking laminated menu cards and rounded diner signage rather than sharp corporate rectangles. Interactive chips, badges, and primary/secondary buttons are full pills (`999px`), like loyalty-card stamps or rank medals. The checkerboard motif (alternating `cream-counter`/`checker-light` squares) appears only as a thin divider strip or footer/header band accent — never as a full-page background, where it would overwhelm content.

## Components

### Buttons
- **Shape:** full pill (`999px` radius), 2px `gravy-ink` border, Sticker shadow at rest.
- **Primary:** `fry-gold` background, `gravy-ink` text, Title typography, 12px/28px padding. Reserved for the one primary action per screen (Submit, Approve).
- **Secondary:** `paper-white` background, `gravy-ink` text and border, same shape/padding — used for all non-primary actions.
- **Destructive/Alert:** same shape, `ketchup-red` background, `paper-white` text — reject, delete, cancel actions only.
- **Hover / Focus:** background shifts to the `-deep` variant; shadow grows to Sticker Lifted; focus ring is a 3px `gravy-ink` outline offset 2px, never a soft glow.

### Chips (tags, status)
- **Style:** `checker-light` background, `gravy-text` label type, full pill, no border (chips are quieter than cards/buttons).
- **State:** status chips swap fill color by meaning — `mustard-amber` for in-review, `relish-green` for approved, `ketchup-red` for rejected — always paired with a text label, never color alone.

### Cards / Containers
- **Corner Style:** `md` (12px) for poutine/review cards, `lg` (20px) for hero/leaderboard-winner cards.
- **Border/Shadow:** 2px `gravy-ink` border + Sticker shadow at rest, Sticker Lifted on hover for anything clickable.
- **Content Rhythm:** image/photo first (poutine photo), Title below, meta row (rating score, tag chips) beneath that, using `sm`–`md` internal spacing.

### Leaderboard / Rank Badges
- **Shape:** circular, 40px, `fry-gold` fill, `gravy-ink` border, Score typography centered.
- **Top-1 treatment:** the current season/all-time #1 gets a `mustard-amber` ring accent outside the badge border — the closest this system gets to a literal medal, used sparingly (only true #1 placements, never generic "featured" tagging).

### Map & List Views (Employee app discovery)
- **List rows:** card treatment above, one row per poutine, rank/score right-aligned in Score typography.
- **Map pins:** circular `fry-gold`-filled pins with `gravy-ink` border matching the rank-badge shape language, so map and list feel like one system, not two.

## Do's and Don'ts
